## Purpose

This SOP describes the procedures for obtaining site access and
research permits for field work conducted by the EA Program. Field
research on public or institutional lands almost always requires
advance authorization [@usfws_edna2019]. Working without proper permits
can result in fines, confiscation of samples, invalidation of data,
and jeopardized relationships with land managers. This document
provides an agency-by-agency guide covering the landowners and managers
most commonly encountered by EA Program researchers.


## Scope

- **Applies to:** All EA Program field activities that take place on
  lands managed by the agencies and institutions listed in this SOP,
  including class field trips, independent student research, and
  faculty-led projects
- **Does not apply to:** Laboratory procedures; field work on private
  land (which requires landowner permission negotiated on a
  case-by-case basis); marine or offshore research (which may require
  additional permits from NOAA or the California Coastal Commission)
- **Key principle:** It is the responsibility of the PI (or the
  supervising faculty member) to determine what permits are required
  and to obtain all necessary approvals before any field work begins.
  Students should never assume that their faculty advisor has obtained
  permits -- always confirm.


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Faculty      | Identify required permits, submit applications, maintain permit files, ensure compliance with all permit conditions |
| Field Lead        | Carry copies of active permits in the field; confirm permit status before each outing |
| Students          | Verify that permits are in place before field work; follow all permit conditions; report any compliance issues to the PI |


## Definitions

- **BFS (Bernard Field Station):** An 86-acre biological reserve of
  The Claremont Colleges located at 1400 N. Amherst Avenue, Claremont,
  CA; administered by the BFS Director; all organized access requires
  an approved Use Request [@bfs_userequest].
- **CESA (California Endangered Species Act):** California state law
  (Fish and Game Code §2050 et seq.) that protects state-listed
  threatened and endangered species; take of CESA-listed species
  requires a separate Memorandum of Understanding from CDFW in
  addition to a Scientific Collecting Permit [@cdfw_scp].
- **CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit (SCP):** A permit issued by the
  California Department of Fish and Wildlife authorizing the take or
  possession of wildlife for scientific, educational, or propagation
  purposes; required whenever research involves capturing, handling,
  marking, or collecting wildlife, or when take of sensitive species
  may occur incidentally [@cdfw_scp].
- **ESA Section 10 permit:** A federal incidental take permit issued
  by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service under Section 10(a)(1)(A)
  of the Endangered Species Act; required for non-federal activities
  that involve take of federally listed threatened or endangered
  species [@usfws_esa_s10].
- **ESA Section 7 consultation:** The formal interagency process under
  Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act through which a federal
  agency (e.g., USFS, BLM) consults with USFWS or NMFS to ensure
  that its authorized activities do not jeopardize listed species or
  destroy critical habitat.
- **Incidental take:** The unintentional, but not unexpected, harm to
  a listed species that results from an otherwise lawful activity;
  must be authorized through a Section 10 permit (private activities)
  or Section 7 consultation (federal activities).
- **NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act):** Federal law requiring
  federal agencies to assess the environmental impacts of their
  proposed actions; complex research proposals on federal lands may
  trigger NEPA review, substantially extending the permit processing
  timeline.
- **RAMS (Reserve Application Management System):** The online portal
  through which researchers and instructors apply for access to
  University of California Natural Reserve System reserves
  [@ucnrs_guidelines].
- **RPRS (Research Permit and Reporting System):** The National Park
  Service's online system for submitting research permit applications,
  reporting annual activities, and communicating with park research
  coordinators [@nps_rprs].
- **Special Use Permit (SUP):** A general-purpose permit issued by
  federal land management agencies (BLM, USFS) authorizing a
  specific research project or activity on public lands; may take
  60--120 days or more to process [@blm_science; @usfs_permits].
- **Take:** Under California Fish and Game Code §86, to hunt, pursue,
  catch, capture, or kill, or attempt to do so; under the federal
  ESA, to harass, harm, pursue, hunt, shoot, wound, kill, trap,
  capture, or collect, or attempt to do so.
- **UC Natural Reserve System (UCNRS):** A network of 41+ reserves
  managed by the University of California for research, teaching, and
  public service; access requires an approved RAMS application
  [@ucnrs_guidelines].


## General Principles

### Planning Timeline

Permit processing times vary widely. Submit applications at least
60--90 days before the planned start of field work. Some agencies
(particularly federal ones involving NEPA review or listed species)
may require 6 months or more. Always confirm the current timeline
with the specific office.

| Agency / Institution       | Typical Lead Time      |
|:---------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Bernard Field Station      | 1--2 weeks             |
| California State Parks     | 60--90 days            |
| UC Natural Reserve System  | 2--4 weeks             |
| CDFW (General Use SCP)     | 60--90 days            |
| CDFW (Specific Use SCP)    | 3--6 months            |
| USFWS (Section 10)         | 3--12 months           |
| BLM                        | 60--120 days           |
| National Park Service      | 60--120 days           |
| USDA Forest Service        | 60--120 days           |

### Permits You May Need Simultaneously

A single field project can require permits from multiple agencies. For
example, sampling macroinvertebrates in a stream within a National
Forest may require a USFS Special Use Permit, a CDFW Scientific
Collecting Permit, and (if listed species are present) a USFWS Section
10 permit. The land management agency will typically not finalize its
own permit until copies of all other required permits are submitted.

### Permit Files

The PI must maintain a digital folder (in the EA Program Google Drive
or GitHub repository) containing:

- Copies of all active permits (signed, final versions)
- Copies of all applications submitted
- Copies of annual reports and compliance documents submitted to
  agencies
- Expiration dates and renewal deadlines

Field leads must carry printed or digital copies of relevant permits
during every field outing.

### Insurance and Liability

Several agencies require proof of liability insurance as a condition
of permit issuance. Pomona College maintains institutional liability
coverage; contact the Office of Risk Management to obtain a
Certificate of Insurance naming the specific agency as an additional
insured party.


## Agency-Specific Procedures

### Robert J. Bernard Biological Field Station (BFS)

The BFS is an 86-acre facility of The Claremont Colleges located at
1400 N. Amherst Avenue, Claremont, CA. Access requires advance
approval from the BFS Director [@bfs_userequest].

**When a permit is needed:** All research projects, class field trips,
and organized activities on the BFS require a Use Request, even for
Claremont Colleges faculty and students. Casual, unaccompanied
pedestrian access also requires prior authorization.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the BFS Director (Dr. Wallace M. Meyer III,
   wallace.meyer\@pomona.edu, 909-621-8577) to discuss the proposed
   project
2. Complete the online "Apply to Use" form at
   <https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/using-the-bfs/>
3. Allow 1--2 weeks for approval; more complex projects may require
   additional review

**Website:** <https://bfs.sites.pomona.edu/using-the-bfs/>

---

### California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW)

CDFW issues Scientific Collecting Permits (SCPs) for the take or
possession of wildlife (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish,
certain plants, and invertebrates) for scientific, educational, and
propagation purposes [@cdfw_scp].

**When a permit is needed:** Any time your research involves
capturing, handling, marking, or collecting wildlife -- or when there
is potential for incidental take of sensitive species.

**Permit types:**

- **General Use SCP** -- for more common species, non-invasive
  methods, and areas outside Marine Protected Areas
- **Specific Use SCP** -- for focused studies involving prohibited
  wildlife, more invasive methods, or sensitive locations including
  MPAs

**How to apply:**

1. Review the SCP regulations (Title 14, Section 650, CCR) and
   Standard Conditions at <https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting>
2. Apply online through the Scientific Collecting Permit Portal (SCPP)
3. Pay the required permit fee before issuance

**CESA-listed species:** Requires a separate CESA Memorandum of
Understanding from CDFW in addition to the SCP.

**Reporting:** Each permitholder must submit a Mandatory Wildlife
Report (form DFW 1379a) annually.

**Website:** <https://wildlife.ca.gov/Licensing/Scientific-Collecting>

---

### California Department of Parks and Recreation (State Parks)

**When a permit is needed:** Any scientific research, data collection,
specimen collection, or installation of monitoring equipment in
California State Park System lands requires written authorization
[@caparks_research].

**How to apply:**

1. Download and complete form DPR 65 from
   <https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557>
2. Prepare a full study proposal following the Study Proposal
   Guidelines for Research in California State Parks
3. Submit the application, study proposal, proof of insurance, and
   copies of any other required permits (CDFW, USFWS, etc.) to the
   appropriate State Parks district office; for multi-district
   projects, submit to the Natural Resources Division in Sacramento at
   nrd.research\@parks.ca.gov
4. Allow 60--90 days for processing

**Reporting:** A summary report of activities and findings must be
submitted to State Parks; renewal is contingent on receipt of this
report.

**Website:** <https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=21557>

---

### University of California Natural Reserve System (UCNRS)

The UCNRS manages 41+ reserves across California for research,
teaching, and public service [@ucnrs_guidelines].

**When a permit is needed:** All research projects and class visits
require an approved application through the Reserve Application
Management System (RAMS).

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the reserve director(s) to discuss project requirements
2. Review the NRS Use Guidelines at
   <https://ucnrs.org/reserve-research-guidelines/>
3. Submit a research application through RAMS at
   <https://rams.ucnrs.org>
4. Once approved, submit a Reservation for each planned visit through
   RAMS

**Special conditions:**

- IACUC approval required if the project involves vertebrate animals
- Additional agency permits (CDFW, USFWS) may be required
- All equipment must be removed and sites restored at project
  conclusion

**Website:** <https://ucnrs.org/>

---

### U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS)

USFWS administers permits for activities involving species listed
under the federal Endangered Species Act (ESA), migratory birds
(Migratory Bird Treaty Act), and wildlife on National Wildlife Refuges
[@usfws_esa_s10].

**When a permit is needed:**

- Take of federally listed threatened or endangered species requires
  a Section 10(a)(1)(A) recovery permit
- Research involving migratory birds requires a federal Bird Banding
  Permit and/or Scientific Collecting Permit
- Research on National Wildlife Refuge lands requires a Special Use
  Permit from the refuge manager

**How to apply:**

1. For ESA-listed species: submit form 3-200-55 through the USFWS
   Endangered Species permits portal
2. For migratory birds: apply through the USFWS Bird Banding
   Laboratory or the federal permits portal
3. For refuge access: contact the specific refuge manager

**Key considerations:** Section 10 applications are subject to a
30-day Federal Register public comment period; processing times are
3--12 months. Annual reports are required for all active permits.

**Website:** <https://www.fws.gov/service/apply-permit>

---

### Bureau of Land Management (BLM)

BLM manages extensive public lands in California, including desert,
grassland, and mountain areas where EA Program research may occur
[@blm_science].

**When a permit is needed:** Any organized research activity on
BLM-managed lands, including specimen collection, installation of
monitoring equipment, and systematic surveys.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the nearest BLM Field Office at
   <https://www.blm.gov/office/directory>
2. BLM staff will determine whether a Special Recreation Permit,
   research authorization, or another approval type is needed
3. Submit required application materials (maps, project description,
   copies of other agency permits)
4. Allow 60--120 days; complex NEPA projects may take longer

**Website:** <https://www.blm.gov/learn/science-in-the-blm/conducting-science>

---

### National Park Service (NPS)

NPS requires a Scientific Research and Collecting Permit for most
scientific activities in any unit of the National Park System
[@nps_rprs].

**When a permit is needed:** Any study in the natural or social
sciences within a national park, monument, seashore, or other NPS
unit.

**How to apply:**

1. Create an investigator account in the Research Permit and
   Reporting System (RPRS) at <https://irma.nps.gov/rprs/>
2. Locate the park profile in RPRS and contact the research
   coordinator for park-specific conditions
3. Submit the application through RPRS; allow 60--120 days
4. Annual reports are submitted through RPRS

**Website:** <https://www.nps.gov/subjects/science/research-and-collecting-permit-overview.htm>

---

### USDA Forest Service (USFS)

USFS manages National Forest System (NFS) lands through local Ranger
District offices [@usfs_permits].

**When a permit is needed:** Any organized research activity on NFS
lands, including specimen collection, installation of monitoring
equipment, and systematic surveys.

**How to apply:**

1. Contact the Ranger District office for the relevant National
   Forest (for Southern California: San Bernardino, Angeles,
   Cleveland, or Los Padres)
2. Download and complete a Research Special-Use Operating
   Plan/Itinerary from the forest's website and submit it to the
   district permit coordinator
3. Forest staff will determine whether a full Special Use Permit or a
   Research Permit Waiver is appropriate
4. Allow 60--120 days; projects requiring NEPA analysis may take
   longer

**Special conditions:**

- Projects involving wildlife or threatened/endangered plants may
  require additional CDFW and/or USFWS authorization
- A summary of findings must be provided to the Forest Service upon
  completion

**Website:** <https://www.fs.usda.gov/>


## Permit Decision Flowchart

Use the following steps to determine what permits you need:

1. **Identify the land manager.** Who owns or manages the land where
   you will work?
2. **Obtain the land access permit** from the land manager (Sections
   5.1--5.8 above).
3. **Will you handle, capture, collect, or disturb wildlife?** If yes,
   you likely need a CDFW Scientific Collecting Permit (§5.2).
4. **Are any federally listed species present, or could they be
   incidentally encountered?** If yes, you likely need a USFWS Section
   10 permit or ESA Section 7 consultation (§5.5).
5. **Are any state-listed species (CESA) present?** If yes, you need
   a CESA MOU from CDFW in addition to the SCP (§5.2).
6. **Does the land manager require other agency permits before issuing
   its own?** If yes, obtain those permits first and submit copies
   with your land access application.

::: {.callout-tip}
### When in doubt, ask
If you are unsure whether a permit is required, contact the agency
before beginning field work. It is always better to ask in advance
than to be stopped in the field or have your data and specimens
invalidated.
:::

## Training Record

Before leading field work on any permitted site, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Identify all permits required for their specific project and site
3. Confirm with the PI that all permits are active and in hand
4. Know where to find copies of active permits (digital and/or
   printed)
5. Understand the reporting requirements for each active permit
6. Be signed off by the PI or designated field lead
